comments.comment: Badly Drawn Turtle People can be very rational. Being rational is just a way of thinking, in this context basing your judgment on the evidence and things relevant to the case presented in court rather than prejudice or outside knowledge.  While people can often be stupid, experience suggests that people actually take their role on juries quite seriously.  And computers would be great at being jurors if you could assign mathematical values to evidence. But you can't. Example:  V was shot, allegedly by D, on the corner of Bert St and Russell St at around 9pm. A, who was walking his dog at the time, says he saw a man wearing a black hoodie and jeans, with what A believes was a gold watch, shoot V at close range, and then run off. The police searched D's house and found that he owns a black hoodie and jeans. D also wears a watch. B, a neighbour on the corner of Bert and Russell, says she saw 4 men standing on the street corner at around 8:55, all wearing hoodies and jeans. B saw one of these men leave and then at 9pm heard a gunshot and saw 2 men in hoodies and jeans running down Bert St. Y, D's friend, says that D was at Y's house all night on the night of the shooting. X, another of D's friends that is known to the police as a gang member in the area, says that at around 8:50 he was at a convenience store with D, but not Y, on the night of the shooting, just 10 minutes walk from Bert and Russell.  D has an extensive criminal record, but has no convictions for violent crimes. The defence instructs the jury that it was dark, so that both A and B's evidence may not be reliable, even though they gave their evidence with confidence. During cross examination, it also emerges that A wears glasses, but he cannot recall whether he was wearing his glasses the night of the shooting.  How would you get a computer to take into account all of this information and compute it to reach a verdict? How would a computer assess the reliability of witnesses, given notions of imperfect recollection, how confident they appeared of their evidence in court, whether they would have a motive to lie, who would be lying, etc.?
